title: The relational model, keys and NULL
goal: By the end, you can say what a database, a table and a query are, pick a table's keys, predict what an empty value (NULL) does to a filter and a count, and write a one-table query with the right time range, order and number of rows.
opening:
Picture a small company whose app records card payments at cafés and shops: which card, which shop, how much and when. It also lists its 13 customers, noting who invited each one.

Asha's two friends got a free coffee when they joined with her invitation. Now the company wants to send one to everybody else: every customer Asha didn't invite. You ask the database for that list, and it answers at once, with no error.

It's easy to trust an answer like that. The question reads like plain English, so the answer should mean what the English means. But a database reads a question by stricter rules.

Containers are processes, the last lesson of the Operating systems track, showed that a container is an ordinary program with a private view of the computer. Part II, Data on one machine, starts with a database that runs in one. In this lesson, we'll meet its tables, keys and empty values, and the order in which it reads a question. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The customers table has 13 rows. Its column `referred_by` holds the id of the customer who invited each one, or nothing at all when nobody did. Asha, customer 1, invited 2 customers, other customers invited 6, and 5 were invited by nobody. How many rows does `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE referred_by <> 1` return? (`<>` means "not equal to".)
options: None: the database stops with an error when it meets an empty value
warmup.why: The 2 customers Asha invited give false: their `referred_by` is 1. The 5 empty ones hold NULL, SQL's marker for "no value here", and comparing NULL with 1 gives neither true nor false, but unknown. WHERE keeps only the rows where the test is true, so only the 6 customers invited by somebody else come back. Nothing raises an error: the 5 rows disappear without a word. That's why 11, the number the English question means, is so tempting. The fourth section explains the rule, and how to get 11.

sections.h: A database keeps the payments in tables, and a query asks for them
sections.body:
Let's start with the smallest program that could record payments: a list in the computer's memory. When the program stops, the list is gone. So the next version adds one line per payment to a file, as What a data system is, the first lesson of this course, did. The payments now survive a restart, and new problems appear. To find one card's payments, the program reads the whole file. Two copies of the program writing at once can mix their half-written lines. Nothing stops a bug from writing a payment for card 99, which doesn't exist. And every new question, such as "the five biggest payments in March", means new code.

A **database** is a program whose whole job is to keep data safe and answer questions about it. This course uses PostgreSQL 18, a free database program that many companies run. It works as a **server**: a program that runs all the time, owns its data files and answers requests. Other programs never touch those files; they send the server requests. psql is one of them: a small program that comes with PostgreSQL, where you type requests and read the answers.

Inside the database, data sits in **tables**. A table looks like one sheet of a spreadsheet. Its **columns** have names and types: whole numbers, text, a moment in time. Each **row** records one fact. Here are four of the eight shops in the `merchants` table (the payments app calls a shop a merchant):

| merchant_id | name | country_code |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Northwind Grocers | US |
| 2 | Blue Fern Cafe | GB |
| 4 | Volt Electronics | DE |
| 6 | Paper Lantern Books | IN |

The `course` database holds a small, made-up copy of the coffee-shop payments app. Besides `merchants`, there's `customers`, one row per person who signed up, and `accounts`, one row per pot of money with a balance. Customers own accounts, and so do the shops, which is where their takings land. `cards` has one row per card, and each card draws on one account. `payments` has one row per tap of a card.

You ask for data with a **query**, a question written in **SQL**, the language almost every database of this kind understands. Here's one, typed into psql. `course=#` is psql's prompt, and `course-#` means the question carries on from the line above:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT payment_id, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, status, created_at
course-# FROM payments
course-# WHERE payment_id = 17;
 payment_id | card_id | merchant_id | amount_minor |  status   |       created_at
------------+---------+-------------+--------------+-----------+------------------------
         17 |       8 |           4 |        18999 | succeeded | 2026-03-12 16:40:00+00
(1 row)
```

Read it like a sentence. `SELECT` names the columns, `FROM` names the table and `WHERE` says which rows. The answer is a small table of its own: a header, one row and a count. That row is one fact: card 8 paid shop 4, Volt Electronics, 189.99 on 12 March 2026 at 16:40 UTC, the world's reference clock. Amounts are stored in cents, because whole numbers add up exactly and a computer's fractions sometimes don't. The database also checks **constraints**, rules it applies to every write, such as "a payment's card must exist". The third section uses one to end the card 99 problem.

Notice what the query leaves out: which file to open, where payment 17 sits, how to find it. Ordering at a café counter works the same way. You say "a flat white, please", and the barista decides which cup, which machine and which steps. This style of asking is called **declarative**: you describe the result, and the database works out the steps.

Data kept in tables and asked declarative questions is the relational model. E. F. Codd, a researcher at IBM, published it in 1970, and he called a table a relation, hence "relational database". Go deeper tells what it replaced.

The picture for this whole track fits in two sentences. **A table is a pile of facts. Keys say which fact is which and how facts point at each other, and a query filters and reshapes the facts in a fixed order.** Let's take it one word at a time, starting with "pile".

refs.title: E. F. Codd, A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks (1970)

aside.title: Isn't a table the same as a spreadsheet?
aside.body: For reading a few rows, the picture holds, and it's a good one to keep. The differences show up when many programs use the data at once. A spreadsheet file is usually changed by one person at a time, while a database server answers thousands of programs and keeps their changes apart. A spreadsheet accepts whatever you type into a cell, while a database refuses a row that breaks one of its rules. And a sheet in Excel, Microsoft's spreadsheet program, stops at 1,048,576 rows, while a database keeps billions of rows on disk and reads only the parts a question needs.

sections.h: A table is a bag of rows, and it has no order
sections.body:
Ask for the country of each customer who joined before 2026: `SELECT country_code FROM customers WHERE created_at < '2026-01-01'`. Five rows come back, and US appears twice, because two of those five customers live in the US. A mathematician would frown. Codd took the word relation from mathematics, where a relation is a set of rows: no row appears twice, and there's no first or last. SQL keeps neither promise.

A SQL table is a **bag**: a collection that can hold the same thing twice, like a shopping bag with two identical apples in it. Answers are bags too. `SELECT DISTINCT` drops the repeats and returns four rows, in the order US, FR, IN, DE. That's neither alphabetical nor the order the customers joined. To find the repeats, PostgreSQL put each value into a numbered bucket, chosen by a number worked out from the value (a hash table), and then handed the buckets back in bucket order.

Order is the bigger trap. PostgreSQL stores a table in a file made of pages, blocks of 8 KB that it always reads and writes whole. All 13 customers fit in one page. With no shortcut to the right rows, PostgreSQL reads the pages from first to last, a **sequential scan**, and returns rows in the order it meets them. Its documentation promises only that rows come back "in whatever order the system finds fastest to produce".

On a fresh table, that looks like the order the rows went in, until a row moves. PostgreSQL never changes a row where it sits. An `UPDATE`, the SQL command that changes rows, writes a new copy of the row, usually after the others, and the next scan meets it last. (The old copy stays for a while, for queries that are still reading it. The Transactions track explains why.)

A café counter works the same way: drinks come out in the order they're ready, unless somebody sets a rule. In SQL, the rule is `ORDER BY`. Without it, `LIMIT 3`, which keeps the first three rows of an answer, means "any three rows". A test, a small program that checks a query's answer, can expect the three oldest customers and pass for months, until somebody updates one of them.

**Rows have no order until you ask for one. Write ORDER BY.**

The Try it below moves a row on purpose. Sorting by `customer_id` fixes the order, because no two customers share an id. So what makes one row different from every other? Next, we'll look at keys.

try.title: Watch a row move
steps: From the `labs` folder, start the course database: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml up -d`. Docker is a program that runs other programs inside containers, and this command starts PostgreSQL 18 in one. The first start creates the payments tables and fills them with a small set of made-up rows in a few seconds.

Open psql on it: `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml exec db psql -U sfz -d course`. Here `-U sfz` is the user name and `-d course` picks the database. Then type `\pset null '∅'`, so empty values print as ∅ for the rest of the lesson. The fourth section explains them.
Run the first `SELECT` and note the three ids. Predict: after an `UPDATE` that sets a name to itself, and so changes nothing, will the same query return the same three rows?
Run the rest, one statement at a time. `BEGIN` starts a transaction, a group of changes that becomes permanent only on `COMMIT`. `ROLLBACK` throws the group away, so the database stays as it was.

code.title: psql, database course

try.expect:
The first query returns customers 1, 2 and 3. After the update, the same query returns 2, 3 and 4:

```postgresql
course=*# SELECT customer_id, full_name FROM customers LIMIT 3;
 customer_id |  full_name
-------------+--------------
           2 | Ben Carter
           3 | Chloe Martin
           4 | Daniel Kim
(3 rows)
```

The update wrote a new copy of customer 1 after the other rows, so the scan reached it last. The query with `ORDER BY customer_id` returns 1, 2 and 3 both times. The `*` in the prompt, `course=*#`, means a transaction is open.

sections.h: Keys decide when two rows are the same fact
sections.body:
Payments 17 and 18 look alike. Same card, same shop, same amount, two minutes apart:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT payment_id, card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor, created_at
course-# FROM payments
course-# WHERE card_id = 8 AND merchant_id = 4
course-# ORDER BY payment_id;
 payment_id | card_id | merchant_id | amount_minor |       created_at
------------+---------+-------------+--------------+------------------------
         17 |       8 |           4 |        18999 | 2026-03-12 16:40:00+00
         18 |       8 |           4 |        18999 | 2026-03-12 16:42:10+00
(2 rows)
```

Card 8 belongs to Farid Haddad. Did he buy the same thing twice, or was one purchase written down twice? Two identical receipts in a wallet raise the same question. To answer it, a table needs a rule that says which row is which: a key. We'll build one in three tries.

First try: tell payments apart by what they say, `(card_id, merchant_id, amount_minor)`. Payments 17 and 18 share all three, so the rule breaks at once. Add the time, and `(card_id, created_at)` is unique in the current data. That still isn't a rule. A program copying in payments from elsewhere could write two rows with the same time, and nothing would stop it. Data can show that some columns aren't unique. It can never show that they always will be.

A **superkey** is a set of columns whose values never repeat across rows, and never will. A **candidate key** is a superkey with nothing to spare: drop any one column and it stops being unique. `(payment_id, status)` is a superkey, but `status` adds nothing, so the pair isn't a candidate key. `payment_id` alone is one.

Second try: let the database number the rows, like a bakery's numbered tickets. `payment_id` is an **identity column**: for each new row, PostgreSQL takes the next number from a counter called a sequence. A key with no meaning outside the database is a **surrogate key**. Now every row has a name, but a retry still looks like a new payment. A card reader sends a payment, the server stores it, and the answer is lost on the way back. The reader gives up waiting and sends it again. The server stores it as row 38 with a fresh number, and the card is charged twice.

Third try: let the card reader name the payment. `payment_uid` is a **UUID**, a 128-bit identifier any program can make on its own, so random that two will almost never match. It's written as 32 hexadecimal digits (0 to 9, then a to f), such as `019ce2eb-5700-7011-8000-000000000011`. The reader makes it once and sends it with every attempt. A name that lets the server carry out a request once, however often it arrives, is an **idempotency key**. A `UNIQUE` constraint on the column makes the second insert, the attempt to add the same row again, fail. PostgreSQL checks it with a **B-tree index**, a sorted structure that maps each key to where its row lives, like the index at the back of a book. So the check reads a few 8 KB pages, not the whole table.

`payments` now has two candidate keys. You pick one as the **primary key** (PK in the figure), the table's main name for a row. PostgreSQL makes its columns `NOT NULL`, so they must always hold a value, and gives it a unique index. Protect every other candidate key with `UNIQUE`.

That leaves card 99. A **foreign key** (FK) solves it. `payments.card_id REFERENCES cards` means every `card_id` in payments must exist as a key in cards. PostgreSQL checks it on every insert or update in payments, and on every delete in cards. Foreign keys are also how the tables point at each other: a payment at its card and its shop, a card at its account, an account at its customer or its shop. The figure shows the five core tables, and psql's `\d payments`, which describes a table, lists the keys (output trimmed):

```postgresql
course=# \d payments
...
Indexes:
    "payments_pkey" PRIMARY KEY, btree (payment_id)
    "payments_payment_uid_key" UNIQUE CONSTRAINT, btree (payment_uid)
Foreign-key constraints:
    "payments_card_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (card_id) REFERENCES cards(card_id)
    "payments_merchant_id_fkey" FOREIGN KEY (merchant_id) REFERENCES merchants(merchant_id)
```

Notice what's missing: there's no index on `card_id` or `merchant_id`. A foreign key doesn't create one, so finding one card's payments still reads the whole table. Indexes and reading EXPLAIN, in the Storage engines track, shows what that costs.

**Data can break a key, but it can't prove one. Declare the keys you mean.**

Some rows, though, have a column with nothing in it at all. Next, we'll see what an empty value does to a question.

try.title: Break the keys on purpose
steps: Payment 17 has the `payment_uid` `019ce2eb-5700-7011-8000-000000000011`. Predict what happens when a card reader's retry sends that uid again.
Run the two inserts below. `INSERT INTO ... VALUES` adds a row, and `now()` is the current time. Each error names the constraint that stopped it.
Run `\d cards` and find the foreign key that points at accounts.

code.title: psql, database course

try.expect:
Both inserts fail, and nothing is written:

```text
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "payments_payment_uid_key"
DETAIL:  Key (payment_uid)=(019ce2eb-5700-7011-8000-000000000011) already exists.

ERROR:  insert or update on table "payments" violates foreign key constraint "payments_card_id_fkey"
DETAIL:  Key (card_id)=(99) is not present in table "cards".
```

The second insert gave no `payment_uid`, so the column's default, `uuidv7()`, made a fresh one. That function is new in PostgreSQL 18, and it makes UUIDs that start with the current time. So the second insert failed on the card, not on the uid.

sections.h: NULL means unknown, and WHERE keeps only true
sections.body:
The app runs an invite-a-friend offer, so each row in `customers` has a column called `referred_by`: the id of the customer who invited this one. Asha Rao, customer 1, invited Chloe and Elena. Kofi Mensah, customer 11, signed up without an invitation. What should his `referred_by` hold?

Try the first answers that come to mind. `0` fails at once: there's no customer 0, so the foreign key rejects it. And if it didn't, a count of invited customers would count Kofi. A made-up value such as `-1` has the same problems, and every query must remember what `-1` means. SQL's answer is a marker that means "no value here": **NULL**.

Picture NULL as a sealed envelope. There may be a number inside, but nobody can see it. Is the envelope equal to 1? The honest answer is "can't tell", and that's the answer SQL gives. Ask whether NULL equals 1, and SQL doesn't say false. It says NULL again, which here means **unknown**. Logic with three answers, true, false and unknown, is called **three-valued logic**. Here are its rules in one query. `AS` names each answer column, `::boolean` makes the last NULL a true-or-false value, and psql prints NULL as ∅ because of `\pset null '∅'`:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT NULL = NULL AS "null = null", NULL <> 1 AS "null <> 1", NULL IS NULL AS "is null",
course-#        NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 1 AS "distinct from 1", true OR NULL AS "true or null",
course-#        false AND NULL AS "false and null", NOT NULL::boolean AS "not null";
 null = null | null <> 1 | is null | distinct from 1 | true or null | false and null | not null
-------------+-----------+---------+-----------------+--------------+----------------+----------
 ∅           | ∅         | t       | t               | t            | f              | ∅
(1 row)
```

Read each column as a rule. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, whether it's `=`, `<>` (not equal), `<` or `>`. That includes `NULL = NULL`: two sealed envelopes may or may not hold the same number. `IS NULL` asks a different question, "is this a sealed envelope?", and that question always has an answer. So does `IS DISTINCT FROM`, which treats NULL as an ordinary value, so `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM 1` is true. With `OR` and `AND`, a known side can decide on its own: `true OR unknown` is true whatever the envelope holds, and `false AND unknown` is false. Every other mix with unknown stays unknown, and `NOT unknown` is still unknown.

Now comes the rule that bites. **WHERE keeps a row only when its condition is true.** False and unknown both drop it. So `WHERE referred_by <> 1` drops Kofi and the four other customers nobody invited. In English, Asha didn't invite them, so they belong in the answer. In SQL, their envelopes are sealed, the test is unknown, and the rows fall out with no error and no warning. The stepper below runs that WHERE clause over six rows.

The fix depends on what you mean. `referred_by IS DISTINCT FROM 1` keeps the NULL rows, and so does `referred_by <> 1 OR referred_by IS NULL`. If a column should never be empty, declare it `NOT NULL`, and the question never comes up. The bug feels natural to programmers, because in most languages, Kotlin and Java among them, `null == null` is true. SQL spells that kind of equality `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM`.

The envelope picture breaks in one place: when SQL groups or sorts rows, it puts all the NULLs together, as if they were equal. Go deeper has the details.

Aggregate functions, which fold many rows into one value, have NULL rules of their own. `count(*)` counts rows. `count(referred_by)` counts the rows where `referred_by` isn't NULL. `count(DISTINCT referred_by)` counts the different non-NULL values: here, the customers who invited somebody. On the 13 customers, those are 13, 8 and 7. `sum`, `avg` (the average), `min` and `max` skip NULLs too. And `sum` over no rows at all returns NULL, not 0.

Next, we'll see the order in which PostgreSQL runs the parts of a query, which explains an error that looks impossible.

stepper.title: WHERE referred_by <> 1, one row at a time
stepper.intro: Click Next to watch PostgreSQL test each row. The blue row is the one it decided last; green rows are kept, and dashed red rows are dropped.

sections.h: A SELECT runs in a different order than you write it
sections.body:
This query fails, and the reason teaches one of the most useful rules in SQL. `round(amount_minor / 100.0, 2)` turns cents into an amount with two decimal places, and `AS amount` names the result:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT payment_id, round(amount_minor / 100.0, 2) AS amount
course-# FROM payments
course-# WHERE amount > 500;
ERROR:  column "amount" does not exist
LINE 3: WHERE amount > 500;
              ^
```

`amount` is defined two lines up, so why can't WHERE see it? Because the clause you write first runs late. Picture a barista with a big order for an office. She takes the cups for this order (FROM) and sets aside the ones that aren't hers to make (WHERE). She writes a name on each cup that's left (the select list), lines the cups up by size (ORDER BY) and hands over the first five (LIMIT). She can't set cups aside by a name that isn't written yet. SQL works in the same order, though you write SELECT first. PostgreSQL evaluates the clauses in this logical order:

1. `FROM`, including joins: which rows exist.
2. `WHERE`: keep the rows where the condition is true.
3. `GROUP BY`, then `HAVING`: put rows into groups and filter the groups, the subject of Aggregation, lesson 4 of this track.
4. The select list: compute the output columns and their names.
5. `DISTINCT`: drop repeated output rows.
6. `ORDER BY`: sort.
7. `LIMIT`, `OFFSET` or `FETCH FIRST`: cut the answer to size.

The **planner**, the part of PostgreSQL that decides how to run a query, may do the real work in another order, for example by reading an index instead of scanning the table. That's where the barista picture breaks: she does her steps in order, while the planner only promises an answer that looks as if it had. So a name made in step 4 is invisible in step 2 and visible in step 6: `ORDER BY amount` works. In WHERE, filter on the column itself: `WHERE amount_minor > 50000`.

Step 6 has a trap: ties. Payments 17, 18 and 19 all have `amount_minor = 18999`. With `ORDER BY amount_minor DESC LIMIT 5`, where `DESC` means largest first, any of the three may take the last places, and a different one next week. End the sort with a unique column, `ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id`, and the order is fixed. If you want every tied row, `FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS WITH TIES` (PostgreSQL 13 and later) keeps going until the tie ends.

Step 4 is where `CASE` lives, SQL's version of a chain of if and else. `CASE WHEN amount_minor >= 50000 THEN 'large' ELSE 'small' END` gives each row a label. The first branch whose condition is true wins, and `ELSE` catches the rest. Without an ELSE, the rest get NULL. Watch the short form: `CASE referred_by WHEN NULL THEN ...` compares with `=`, so it never matches a NULL.

Step 2 is where time ranges go wrong. `created_at` is a `timestamptz`: an instant in time, stored in UTC, down to the microsecond. `BETWEEN a AND b` includes both ends, and a date with no time means midnight at its start. So `BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31'` stops at the first instant of 31 March and loses the whole last day. `BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-04-01'` makes the opposite mistake: it includes a payment made at exactly midnight on 1 April. Write every range half-open: `created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01'`. It includes the first instant of March and stops right before the first instant of April, so one month never overlaps the next and never leaves a gap. A date with no time zone is read in the session's `TimeZone` setting, which is UTC in the course database.

**Write time ranges half-open: from the start, up to but not including the end.**

That's the whole one-table query: which rows, which columns, in what order and how many.

try.title: Lose a payment with BETWEEN
steps: Payment 22 was made half a second before midnight on 31 March. Payment 23 was made at exactly midnight on 1 April. Predict which of them each of the first two queries returns.
Run them. Then run the third query and count the rows: you asked for two.
When you're done for the day, leave psql with `\q` and stop the database with `docker compose -f env/postgres.yml down`. Add `-v` to delete the data as well; the next start then loads it fresh.

code.title: psql, database course
code.src:
SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE created_at BETWEEN '2026-03-31' AND '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY created_at;

SELECT payment_id, created_at, amount_minor
FROM payments
WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-31' AND created_at < '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY created_at;

SELECT payment_id, amount_minor FROM payments
WHERE merchant_id = 4 AND created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01'
ORDER BY amount_minor DESC
FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS WITH TIES;

try.expect:
BETWEEN returns both payments, because both ends are included:

```postgresql
 payment_id |        created_at        | amount_minor
------------+--------------------------+--------------
         22 | 2026-03-31 23:59:59.5+00 |        52000
         23 | 2026-04-01 00:00:00+00   |        99000
(2 rows)
```

The half-open range returns only payment 22. The last query returns four rows, not two: payment 15 (89900), then 17, 18 and 19, which tie at 18999 for second place.

compare.title: Empty text and row limits in Oracle and PostgreSQL

a.label: Oracle
a.title: Oracle
a.src:
-- an empty string IS NULL in Oracle
SELECT CASE WHEN '' IS NULL THEN 'null' ELSE 'not null' END AS empty_string
FROM dual;                               -- 'null' (FROM dual is optional from 23ai)

-- so this fails when full_name is NOT NULL
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, email, full_name, country_code)
VALUES (20, 'x@example.com', '', 'US');  -- cannot insert NULL

-- row limits: 12c and later; older code filters on ROWNUM
SELECT payment_id FROM payments
ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;

b.label: PostgreSQL 18
b.title: PostgreSQL 18
b.src:
-- an empty string is a value: length 0, not NULL
SELECT CASE WHEN '' IS NULL THEN 'null' ELSE 'not null' END AS empty_string;
                                         -- 'not null'

-- succeeds and stores a real empty string
INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, email, full_name, country_code)
VALUES (20, 'x@example.com', '', 'US');

-- both spellings work; FETCH FIRST is the standard one
SELECT payment_id FROM payments
ORDER BY amount_minor DESC, payment_id
FETCH FIRST 5 ROWS ONLY;                 -- or LIMIT 5

compare.note: Oracle Database is a commercial database program that many large companies run, and it speaks SQL too. It treats empty text, `''`, as NULL. PostgreSQL follows the SQL standard and keeps `''` and NULL apart: empty text is a value of length 0. So data copied from Oracle arrives with NULL wherever a program once wrote `''`, and code moved from Oracle starts writing empty text that `IS NULL` no longer finds. Pick one meaning per column and enforce it, with `NOT NULL` or `CHECK (col <> '')`. Both databases accept `FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY` and `WITH TIES`; `LIMIT` is PostgreSQL's own spelling. Oracle code older than version 12c limits rows with `ROWNUM`, a number given to each row as it's found. That happens before `ORDER BY` runs, unless you sort in a subquery first.

worked.title: A question from the company, built in the order PostgreSQL runs it

steps.say: Someone at the company asks: which customers joined in the first three months of 2026, leaving out the ones Daniel (customer 4) invited, newest first? And did each of them come through an invitation? Start with FROM and WHERE, and write the three months as a half-open range. Eight customers, 6 to 13, joined in that time.
steps.code:
-- 1. which rows: the quarter, half-open
SELECT customer_id, full_name, referred_by
FROM customers
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01';

steps.say: Leave out Daniel's invitations. `referred_by <> 4` would also drop Grace, Ivy and Kofi, whose `referred_by` is NULL. `IS DISTINCT FROM` keeps them, and drops only Hugo, customer 8.
steps.code:
-- 2. a NULL-safe "not referred by 4"
  AND referred_by IS DISTINCT FROM 4

steps.say: Label each row with a CASE. (`organic` means a customer who came on their own.) The short form looks tidy and is wrong: `CASE referred_by WHEN NULL` compares `referred_by = NULL`, which is never true, so every row falls through to ELSE. On customers 7, 9 and 11, whom nobody invited, it returns `referred` three times. Use the full form, with `IS NULL`.
steps.code:
-- 3. wrong: CASE referred_by WHEN NULL THEN 'organic' ELSE 'referred' END
CASE WHEN referred_by IS NULL THEN 'organic' ELSE 'referred' END AS source

steps.say:
Put it together. The sort ends with `customer_id`, so two customers who joined in the same second still come back in a fixed order. Seven rows: Hugo is the only one left out.

```postgresql
 customer_id |  full_name   | referred_by |  source
-------------+--------------+-------------+----------
          13 | Mateo Ruiz   |           8 | referred
          12 | Lena Novak   |           7 | referred
          11 | Kofi Mensah  |           ∅ | organic
          10 | Jonas Weber  |           5 | referred
           9 | Ivy Chen     |           ∅ | organic
           7 | Grace Lee    |           ∅ | organic
           6 | Farid Haddad |           3 | referred
(7 rows)
```
steps.code:
SELECT customer_id, full_name, referred_by,
       CASE WHEN referred_by IS NULL THEN 'organic' ELSE 'referred' END AS source
FROM customers
WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01'   -- half-open quarter
  AND referred_by IS DISTINCT FROM 4                               -- keeps the NULLs
ORDER BY created_at DESC, customer_id DESC;                        -- unique last key

lab.title: Three one-table queries, checked against the course data
steps: Make sure Docker is running. The tests are small programs that run your queries and compare the answers with the right ones. They start their own PostgreSQL 18 in a container with Testcontainers, a library made for that, and load the same tables and rows as the psql database. So you can try every query in psql first.
Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. All six fail for now. Each failure prints the rows the test expected next to the rows your query returned.
`not_referred_by_asha.sql` holds a query that looks right. Fix its WHERE clause so the customers nobody invited stay in the answer.
In `customer_counts.sql`, give each of the four columns the right kind of count. It stays one SELECT, with no WHERE.
Write `march_top_payments.sql`: the five largest succeeded payments of March 2026, ties broken by `payment_id`, with a `band` column from a CASE.
Run the tests until all six pass. Each exercise has a second test that adds rows first, so an answer typed in by hand fails it.
hints: In psql, `SELECT customer_id, referred_by FROM customers ORDER BY 1;` with `\pset null '∅'` shows exactly which rows are NULL. (`ORDER BY 1` sorts by the first column.)
`count(DISTINCT col)` skips NULLs, like `count(col)`. `count(*) - count(col)` is the number of NULLs in col.
Three payments sit on the edges of March: 13 at 00:00 on 1 March, 22 at 23:59:59.5 on 31 March and 23 at 00:00 on 1 April. Only 13 and 22 are March payments.

drill.title: Write the NULL rules from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking back, write t, f or NULL next to each expression: `NULL = NULL`, `NULL <> 5`, `true AND NULL`, `true OR NULL`, `false AND NULL`, `false OR NULL`, `NOT NULL`, `NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL`. Then write a WHERE clause for a column `fee_minor` that may be NULL: "the fee isn't 500, and a row with no fee counts as not 500".

answer.src:
-- NULL = NULL                -> NULL
-- NULL <> 5                  -> NULL
-- true AND NULL              -> NULL
-- true OR NULL               -> true
-- false AND NULL             -> false
-- false OR NULL              -> NULL
-- NOT NULL                   -> NULL
-- NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL -> false

WHERE fee_minor IS DISTINCT FROM 500
-- or, longer: WHERE fee_minor <> 500 OR fee_minor IS NULL

recap: A database is a server program that owns its data. Other programs send it queries in SQL, which say what they want and never how to find it. The data sits in tables: named, typed columns, and one fact per row.
A SQL table is a bag: repeats stay unless a key or `DISTINCT` removes them, and rows have no order unless you write `ORDER BY`. An `UPDATE` can move a row to the end of the table.

A candidate key is a smallest set of columns that never repeats. Make one the primary key, give every other one a `UNIQUE` constraint, and point from table to table with foreign keys. Data can disprove a key, never prove one.

NULL means unknown: any comparison with it is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows that are true. Say what NULL means with `IS NULL`, `IS DISTINCT FROM` or a `NOT NULL` column. `count(*)` counts rows, `count(col)` counts non-NULL values, and `sum` over no rows is NULL.

PostgreSQL evaluates FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, the select list, DISTINCT, ORDER BY and LIMIT in that order, so WHERE can't see a name made in the select list. End every sort with a unique column, and write time ranges half-open: `>= start AND < end`.

The limit: every query here reads one table, and a payment row says card 8 and shop 4, not who paid or where. Which facts get a table of their own is the next lesson, and putting the tables back together is the one after.
closing:
We started with 13 customers and a free coffee for everyone Asha didn't invite. The database sent back 6 names. The 5 customers nobody invited had a sealed envelope, NULL, in `referred_by`, and WHERE keeps only the rows that are clearly true. `IS DISTINCT FROM 1` brings back all 11.

Open psql on the course database and run `SELECT count(*), count(referred_by) FROM customers;`. The gap between the two numbers is how many rows a careless "not equal" would lose. Next time you write a filter that says "not", ask which side can be empty.

Next, we'll take a messy file of payments where one customer's name has two spellings, and ask how to split it into tables so that each fact lives in one place.

quiz.q: The app keeps refunds, money paid back to a customer, in a table `refunds`. A new column `note_code` may be empty: 36 of the 40 refunds have a code, and 4 have none yet. 10 refunds have `note_code = 'FR'`. How many rows does `SELECT * FROM refunds WHERE note_code <> 'FR'` return?
quiz.why: 30 refunds aren't 'FR', but 4 of those 30 have NULL, and `NULL <> 'FR'` is unknown, so WHERE drops them. 26 remain. 30 is the answer the English question wants, and `note_code IS DISTINCT FROM 'FR'` gives it.

quiz.q: In the current data, no shop has two payments with the same `created_at`. What does that tell you about the pair `(merchant_id, created_at)`?
options: It's a candidate key, so it could be the primary key
It's a foreign key to merchants
Only that it's unique today; it becomes a rule only if you add a UNIQUE constraint
It's a superkey but not a candidate key
quiz.why: A key is a promise about every row the table may ever hold. The current data can show that a set of columns isn't unique, but it can't show that it always will be. Until a UNIQUE constraint enforces it, the next batch of copied-in payments can break it. The first option is the tempting one: it treats the data as if it were the rule.

quiz.q: Why does `SELECT amount_minor / 100 AS amount FROM payments ORDER BY amount` work, while the same query with `WHERE amount > 5` fails?
options: WHERE is evaluated before the select list, and ORDER BY after it
WHERE can't compare numbers that were worked out from a column
Names made in the select list work only in ORDER BY because of a PostgreSQL quirk that other databases don't share
`amount` is a reserved word inside WHERE
quiz.why: The logical order is FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, the select list, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. When WHERE runs, the name `amount` hasn't been made yet. It isn't a quirk of PostgreSQL: other databases, such as Oracle, follow the same rule for the same reason.

quiz.q: A test, a small program that checks a query's answer, runs `SELECT payment_id FROM payments WHERE card_id = 8 LIMIT 1` and expects 6, the card's oldest payment. It has passed 200 times. What's true?
options: It will keep passing, because PostgreSQL returns rows in the order they were added
It can start failing after an update to one of those rows, because without ORDER BY the order is whatever is fastest
LIMIT 1 always returns the row with the lowest primary key
It fails only on PostgreSQL 18, which changed the scan order
quiz.why: Without ORDER BY, rows come back in whatever order the plan produces. An UPDATE writes a new copy of a row elsewhere in the table, and reading through an index instead of the table would change the order again. 200 passes only show that nothing has moved yet. Write `ORDER BY created_at, payment_id`.

quiz.q: Table `t` has three rows whose `score` is 10, 20 and NULL. What does `SELECT count(*), count(score), avg(score) FROM t` return?
quiz.why: `count(*)` counts all three rows. `count(score)` and `avg(score)` skip the NULL, so the average is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15. "3, 2, 10" is what you'd get if NULL counted as zero, which it doesn't.

flashcards.front: What does `NULL = NULL` return in SQL?
flashcards.back: NULL, meaning unknown. Test for it with `IS NULL`, or use `IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` for an equality that treats two NULLs as equal.
Only the rows whose condition is true. Rows where it's false or unknown are dropped, with no error.
Rows; rows where col isn't NULL; different non-NULL values of col. And `sum` over no rows is NULL, not 0.

flashcards.front: In what order do rows come back without ORDER BY?
flashcards.back: In whatever order is fastest for PostgreSQL. It often looks like insertion order until an UPDATE moves a row, so `LIMIT` without `ORDER BY` means any rows.
A candidate key is any smallest set of columns that's unique. The primary key is the one you pick. Give the others a UNIQUE constraint.

flashcards.front: Why can't WHERE use a name made in the select list?
flashcards.back: WHERE runs before the select list, so the name doesn't exist yet. ORDER BY runs after it and can use it.

flashcards.front: How do you select all of March 2026 from a timestamptz column?
flashcards.back: `created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01'`. Half-open: no gap at the end, and no overlap with April.

terms.plain: A question to the database, written in SQL. It says which rows and columns you want, not how to find them.
Named, typed columns and a bag of rows, each row one fact. Codd called it a relation.
A collection that allows repeats. SQL tables and answers are bags unless a key or DISTINCT prevents it.
A smallest set of columns whose values never repeat. A table can have several.
The candidate key you pick as the table's main name for a row. Its columns are NOT NULL and get a unique index.
A column whose values must exist as a key in another table. The database checks it on every write.
Logic with true, false and unknown. Any comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only true.
A range that includes its start and leaves out its end: >= start AND < end.

explain_back.prompt: A friend who's new to databases wrote `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE referred_by <> 1` to list everyone Asha (customer 1) didn't invite. It returns 6 rows, and they expected 11. Explain to them, in your own words, why it happens and how to fix it.
explain_back.answer: `referred_by` is NULL for the five customers nobody invited: the box is empty, not zero. Comparing NULL with 1 gives unknown, not true, and WHERE keeps only the rows where the test is true. So those five rows are dropped, along with the two Asha did invite, which leaves 6. To keep the NULL rows, write `WHERE referred_by IS DISTINCT FROM 1`, which treats NULL as a value that's different from 1, or spell it out as `referred_by <> 1 OR referred_by IS NULL`. Both return 11.

deeper.body:
Codd's model replaced something worth knowing about. The databases of the 1960s stored records in a fixed order, and each record held the address of the next one. A program found a record by following those links, one hop at a time. Change the order, add a shortcut or move the links, and the programs that relied on them broke. Codd's tables have no links and no order: a query says which rows it wants, and the database decides how to find them. That's why a PostgreSQL table can be stored differently, or gain an index, without changing a single query. The name for this is data independence.

NULL isn't treated the same way everywhere in SQL, and the differences are worth knowing before they surprise you.

Comparisons say NULL isn't equal to NULL. Grouping says the opposite: `GROUP BY referred_by` puts all five NULLs into one group, and `DISTINCT` keeps one NULL. Sorting puts NULLs together too. PostgreSQL sorts NULL as larger than every value, so it comes last in ascending order and first in descending order. Oracle Database, a commercial database program, does the same. `NULLS FIRST` and `NULLS LAST` override it:

```postgresql
course=# SELECT referred_by, count(*) FROM customers GROUP BY referred_by ORDER BY referred_by DESC LIMIT 3;
 referred_by | count
-------------+-------
           ∅ |     5
           8 |     1
           7 |     1
(3 rows)
```

A `UNIQUE` constraint goes back to the comparison rules: two NULLs aren't equal, so a unique column accepts any number of NULLs. PostgreSQL 15 added `UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT`, which allows at most one:

```postgresql
course=# CREATE TEMP TABLE t2 (code text UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT);
CREATE TABLE
course=# INSERT INTO t2 VALUES (NULL), (NULL);
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "t2_code_key"
DETAIL:  Key (code)=(null) already exists.
```

Codd's first model, in 1970, had no NULL at all. He added it later, and later still argued for two different markers: one for "there's a value, but we don't know it" (we don't know the customer's phone number) and one for "there's no value to know" (this customer has no inviter, and that's a known fact). SQL has only one NULL, and its logic always treats it as unknown. That's why `referred_by IS NULL` reads as "nobody invited them" in this schema, while `referred_by <> 1` behaves as if the inviter were a secret. When a column's NULL means "doesn't apply", ask whether a real value, a separate table or a `NOT NULL` column with a default would say it more clearly.
